nameStory: The baldcypress gets its name from its unusual habit of shedding all its needles each fall, leaving the tree completely "bald" through winter. Unlike most needle-bearing trees that stay green year-round, this deciduous conifer drops its feathery foliage just like maples and oaks drop their leaves.
description: Baldcypress is a tall, stately tree that can reach 70-100 feet in height with a distinctive buttressed (flared) trunk base. Its soft, feathery needles grow in flat sprays and turn a gorgeous rusty orange before dropping in fall. The tree has a narrow, pyramid shape when young but develops a broader, more irregular crown with age. Despite being native to southern swamps, some baldcypress trees have been planted in New England landscapes.

idTips.label: Needles
idTips.description: Soft, flat needles arranged in feathery sprays along small twigs, bright green in summer turning rusty orange in fall before dropping completely

idTips.label: Trunk Base
idTips.description: Distinctive flared or buttressed base, especially noticeable on older trees, with reddish-brown bark that feels fibrous and peels in long strips

idTips.label: Knees
idTips.description: Woody projections called "cypress knees" may emerge from roots in wet conditions, looking like wooden stalagmites around the tree base

idTips.label: Cones
idTips.description: Round, wrinkled cones about 1 inch across that start green and turn brown, breaking apart on the tree to release seeds

idTips.label: Winter Appearance
idTips.description: Completely bare of needles in winter, showing intricate branching pattern with small twigs that also drop off the tree

habitat: In New England, baldcypress is primarily found as planted ornamental trees in parks, arboretums, and large residential properties, particularly in low-lying or wet areas. They thrive in moist to wet soils and are sometimes planted near ponds, streams, or in rain gardens where their natural love of water can be accommodated.

seasonality.spring: New bright green needles emerge in delicate, feathery sprays, giving the tree a fresh, soft appearance.
seasonality.summer: Full canopy of bright green, feathery foliage creates dense shade and gives the tree its classic pyramid shape.
seasonality.fall: Needles turn brilliant rusty orange or cinnamon brown before dropping completely, creating a carpet of copper-colored foliage below.
seasonality.winter: Tree stands completely bare, revealing its intricate branching structure and distinctive buttressed trunk base.

funFact: Some baldcypress trees are among the oldest living things in North America, with specimens in the wild reaching over 2,000 years old — they were already ancient when the Roman Empire was at its peak!
confusionNotes: The feathery needles might remind you of hemlock, but remember the simple trick: baldcypress needles are flat and soft to the touch, while hemlock needles are attached individually to branches and feel slightly rough. Plus, baldcypress drops all its needles in fall while hemlock stays green year-round.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "cypress," baldcypress is not closely related to the Mediterranean cypress trees you might see in movies. It's also sometimes called "swamp cypress" in reference to its natural habitat in southern wetlands, though the trees planted in New England are usually in regular landscape settings.
compareHints: Baldcypress is the only member of its genus found in New England. Among other conifers in the cypress family, it's most similar to dawn redwood, but baldcypress has needles arranged alternately along twigs while dawn redwood has needles in opposite pairs. Baldcypress also develops the characteristic buttressed trunk base that dawn redwood typically lacks.
